archetype.name: Playoff Team (pass-first)
archetype.definition: A division leader whose record rests on one of the league's most efficient passing attacks, with a middle-of-the-pack defense that makes timely stops rather than controlling games.

report.headline: Burrow's air attack is real; an average defense is finally enough
report.take:
Cincinnati has stopped pretending to be balanced. No offense passes more beyond what the situation calls for (pass rate over expected of 13, first in the league), and few do it better: 0.253 EPA per dropback ranks second, and the overall success rate of 51.5% is also second. Joe Burrow has started every game, Ja'Marr Chase (96 targets) and Tee Higgins (76) take most of the volume, and Chase Brown doubles as a receiving back with 62 targets. Thirty points a game, second in the league, is what that profile produces.

The 7-3 record is mostly earned. The point differential alone implies about 6.1 wins, so the 0.92 wins over expected is a modest bit of good fortune, not a house of cards. What changed from last year's 6-11 is the defense more than the offense. In 2025 it ranked 29th in EPA allowed. This year it sits 16th, and the improvement comes from the edges of the game: a pressure rate that ranks sixth, 13 takeaways (fifth), and a 42.9% red-zone touchdown rate allowed (fifth).

Those edges are also where the numbers flatter it. Down to down, this defense is soft. Opponents succeed on 45% of plays (23rd), convert 47.5% of third downs (30th), and the run defense ranks near the bottom by EPA. Red-zone stops and takeaways swing more from year to year than early-down efficiency, so the points-allowed line is better than the defense underneath it. The run game has a similar gap. Yards before contact rank 26th, but the stuff rate (6th) and short-yardage conversion (4th) are strong, so this is a line that wins in a phone booth and rarely opens anything bigger. Pass protection is middling, with a 23rd-ranked pressure rate allowed and one of the league's slowest times to throw.

From week 7 through week 10 the passing game was overwhelming, posting double-digit pass EPA every week. The loss in Washington showed the formula's limit: with guard Dalton Risner inactive, the run game produced 31 yards and the defense couldn't get off the field. With a one-game lead in the North and a schedule whose only top-tier opponent is Kansas City, this is a playoff team. Whether it is more than that depends on the defense holding up on the plays where it currently gets lucky.

strengths.title: An elite, pass-everything offense
strengths.body: Cincinnati leans on Burrow harder than any team relative to game situation, and the efficiency justifies it: second in pass EPA and in success rate. It runs through two genuine outside threats plus a back who catches, which spreads coverage thin. With Burrow healthy all year and this receiving core intact, it should hold.

strengths.title: Pressure that produces takeaways
strengths.body: The pass rush gets home at a top-six rate, and it shows up as turnovers: 13 takeaways rank fifth. That is the main reason a defense that is average on most snaps still ends drives. Pressure rate is a fairly stable skill. The takeaway rate will probably cool somewhat.

strengths.title: Tight in the red zone, sound deep
strengths.body: Opponents score touchdowns on only 42.9% of red-zone trips, and deep passes against this secondary have been among the least productive in the league. The defense doesn't give up the cheap explosive score, which keeps a high-scoring offense comfortably ahead. Red-zone rates are noisy, though, so treat that half as partly fortune.

concerns.title: Can't get off the field
concerns.body: Opponents convert 47.5% of third downs (30th), and the run defense ranks near the bottom by EPA. That lets offenses sustain drives and shorten the game. It is a real structural flaw, not a role cost. Red-zone stops and turnovers have masked it so far, and that cover won't always be there.

concerns.title: A line that only wins short
concerns.body: Backs average 2.18 yards before contact (26th), and pressure allowed ranks 23rd, made worse by Burrow's long time to throw. When Risner (94% of snaps) sat in Washington, the run game produced 31 yards and the offense became one-dimensional. His knee is the swing item up front.

concerns.title: Soft over the middle
concerns.body: Tight ends have scored 4.3 PPR points a game above their norm against Cincinnati (30th), and short passes do well against it (22nd). The coverage holds up deep and gets picked apart underneath. That combines badly with the third-down problem.

trend.note: After an uneven September that included two losses, the passing game took over from week 7 to week 10, with double-digit pass EPA every week and three comfortable wins. The two-point loss in Washington, with the run game stalled and Risner out, is the only recent dent.

nextGame.headline: Burrow's deep game meets the league's worst deep defense
nextGame.body:
This is close to the ideal matchup for Cincinnati's style. New Orleans allows the worst EPA in the league on deep passes (0.962) and generates the second-lowest pressure rate. Burrow's slow time to throw, a real liability against good fronts, should go largely unpunished. Opposing WR1s have also scored 3.3 PPR points over their norm against the Saints (28th), which points at Chase. The Cincinnati defense's sore spot, the run, matters less here: the Saints' offense ranks 28th in rush EPA and 31st in run success. The Book makes Cincinnati a 10-point home favorite with a 50.5 total.

Availability favors the Bengals. New Orleans is missing right tackle Taliese Fuaga and center Erik McCoy, both near every-snap starters, plus tackle Asim Richards, linebacker Pete Werner and cornerback Martin Emerson Jr. Tight end Juwan Johnson is questionable with a hamstring, which matters given Cincinnati's trouble with tight ends. On the Bengals' side, Risner's return estimate is this week but he is listed out. Cornerback Jalen Davis and safety Kyle Dugger are also listed out, thinning a secondary that will face a Saints team throwing to catch up. Receiver Andrei Iosivas is on IR.

waysToWin.title: Attack the Saints deep
waysToWin.body: New Orleans is the worst deep-pass defense in the league, can't pressure, and is without Emerson at corner. Burrow gets time to wait on Chase and Higgins downfield. An early lead also forces a weak Saints offense into obvious passing downs.

waysToWin.title: Rush a patched-up line
waysToWin.body: With Fuaga and McCoy out, the Saints' protection loses two of its steadiest pieces. Cincinnati's sixth-ranked pressure rate should get home more than usual. Pressure is how this defense creates the takeaways that end games early.

waysToWin.title: Make them beat you through the air
waysToWin.body: The Saints can't run (31st in run success), so Cincinnati's poor run defense is less exposed than usual. That lets the Bengals play coverage on obvious downs without being gashed on the ground.

waysToLose.title: Giveaways keep New Orleans close
waysToLose.body: The 43-36 escape against Tennessee, a team as overmatched as this one, came with four turnovers and no cover as a 13.5-point favorite. The Saints bring down the quarterback at a top-ten sack rate despite rarely pressuring, so holding the ball invites drive-killers. Burrow throwing into one-high looks too eagerly could turn a rout into a coin flip.

waysToLose.title: Third downs and fourth-down aggression
waysToLose.body: Cincinnati's defense allows third-down conversions at the third-worst rate. The Saints have gone for it on every fourth down that qualified. Long Saints drives that end in points rather than punts shorten the game and keep a weak offense in it.

waysToLose.title: Tight ends working the middle
waysToLose.body: Cincinnati's coverage of tight ends ranks 30th, the obvious place for the Saints to move the chains. If Juwan Johnson's hamstring allows him to play, he is the matchup most likely to keep the Saints on schedule.

nextGame.watch: How quickly Chase gets behind a Saints secondary missing Emerson, and whether New Orleans' patched line can give its quarterback time to answer.

restOfSeason.body:
The offense is the part to trust. An elite passing EPA, top-two success rate and a healthy Burrow throwing to Chase and Higgins have been steady across ten games, and only Kansas City on the remaining schedule ranks in the top ten on defense. The run game won't become an asset, but it doesn't need to be.

The defense is where regression lives. A top-five red-zone rate and takeaway count are papering over poor third-down and run defense, so expect points allowed to drift up a little rather than down. The division race is a one-game lead with two games against Cleveland and one against Baltimore still to play. That keeps the margin thin even though the underlying numbers say Cincinnati is the best team in the North.
swingFactors: Risner's return and the run game's floor
Whether red-zone stops and takeaways hold up

confidence.note: Ten games with a stable QB make the offense clear; the defense leans on volatile stats.
